q: A device takes energy of $500\,\text{J}$ and gives useful energy of $350\,\text{J}$ from it. What is its efficiency, and where does the rest of the energy go?
a: $\eta = \dfrac{350\,\text{J}}{500\,\text{J}} = 0.70 = 0.70 \cdot 100\,\% = 70\,\%$. The remaining $500\,\text{J} - 350\,\text{J} = 150\,\text{J}$ is losses, usually heat that spreads into the surroundings. No energy has disappeared, because $350\,\text{J} + 150\,\text{J} = 500\,\text{J}$.

q: The efficiency of a device is $25\,\%$ and it takes a power of $200\,\text{W}$. How large are the useful power and the loss power?
a: The useful power is $P_\text{a} = 0.25 \cdot 200\,\text{W} = 50\,\text{W}$. The loss power is $P_\text{h} = 200\,\text{W} - 50\,\text{W} = 150\,\text{W}$.

q: It is claimed: “A high-power device always has a better efficiency than a low-power device.” Is the claim true? Justify your answer.
a: It is not. Efficiency is the share of the useful power in the power taken, not the power itself. For example, $100\,\text{W}$ and $60\,\text{W}$ incandescent lamps have the same efficiency of about $5\,\%$, even though the high-power lamp takes more power.
